svg.title: AdaGrad: per-parameter effective learning rates, and why they die
svg.desc: A hand-drawn figure. A band at the top gives the rule: G accumulates the squared gradient and the parameter is moved by alpha times the gradient over the root of G plus epsilon, with one cache entry per parameter and epsilon only there to keep the first step finite. The main chart plots the effective rate alpha over root G on log-log axes over ten thousand iterations for two parameters, one with a constant gradient magnitude of two and one of nought point nought two. Both are straight lines of slope minus a half, separated by a factor of a hundred, and neither flattens. A side card names the flaw visible in the same picture: because G only ever grows, every effective rate is on its way to zero, and while the small-gradient parameter keeps a usable rate far longer, given enough steps learning stops for both. A band records that AdaGrad reaches eighty-four per cent after ten thousand epochs against sixty-four point seven for plain SGD and ninety-five point seven for momentum, and that its value here is conceptual.
svg.text: Every parameter sets its own step size
Divide by the root of what each weight has already seen. Then watch what that does over ten thousand steps.

AdaGrad · 84.0% after 10 000 epochs, against 64.7% for plain SGD and 95.7% for momentum.
Its value here is conceptual: the cleanest illustration of per-parameter scaling, before the moving average makes it opaque.
